lesson.title: Fire and Forget: Sockets Without a Connection
lesson.summary: A UDP socket skips the connection setup a TCP socket requires, sending and receiving independent datagrams with an explicit address attached to each one instead.
lesson.body:
A UDP socket is what you get by creating a socket of type SOCK_DGRAM in the Berkeley sockets API. It gives a program the connectionless, unreliable, unordered datagram delivery that UDP provides, a sharp contrast with the connection-oriented TCP socket from the previous chapter.

Because there is no connection to set up, a UDP socket's lifecycle is much simpler. There is no listen() and no accept() at all, since there is no backlog of pending connections to manage when nothing is ever formally connected. connect() can technically still be called on a UDP socket, but it does something different there than it does for TCP: it just records a default destination address locally for convenience, without performing any handshake over the network, since UDP has no handshake to perform. Far more commonly, a UDP program uses sendto() to send a datagram to an address supplied explicitly on that call, and recvfrom() to receive a datagram along with the address it arrived from, since without a connection in place, that is the only way the receiving socket can know who just sent it something.

The contrast with the TCP echo server from the previous chapter is instructive. A UDP echo server creates a socket and calls bind() so it has a known port that clients can reach, exactly as a TCP server would, but from there it simply loops, calling recvfrom(), which hands back both the incoming data and the sender's socket address, and then calling sendto() using that very address to send the echo straight back. There is no accept() step, and no separate socket created per client. The single bound socket handles datagrams from every client that reaches it.

The practical implication is that because there is no connection state being tracked, one socket can receive packets from many different clients, handling each one independently as it arrives, with the address supplied fresh on every call rather than fixed at setup time. It also means it is entirely up to the application to add anything beyond what a single datagram provides, ordering guarantees, retries for lost packets, and so on, since UDP itself will not provide any of that, exactly as covered when UDP was first introduced.
